source.title: Abliterated models are now served cheaply and conveniently via a chat interface - how dangerous are they?

record.tranche_reason: Evaluates the refusal-related behavior of provider-labeled abliterated models in a hosted chat/API setting, rather than reproducing the original direction-finding and ablation procedure.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates whether hosted, provider-labeled abliterated models comply with explicitly dangerous user requests, which bears on V2. Its capability and combined dangerous-capability scores do not test whether a refusal direction was removed or whether abilities were preserved relative to an unabliterated baseline. The Terminal-Bench comparison is attributed to the provider, not reported as the study's own result.
record.test_reason: The study measures compliance on explicitly dangerous bio prompts for two released, hosted models labelled abliterated (r1, r2). That bears weakly on V2's claim that abliteration removes refusal in released models. The evidence is weak for three reasons: there is no unabliterated baseline, the weight edit is not verified, and the judging is self-scored.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. The author also concludes that the hosted models match or exceed FAR.AI's abliterated models on the dangerous-capability proxy, mainly through higher capability. The author calls for regulating commercial providers of abliterated models, at minimum with bioweapons filters, and notes the results do not show end-to-end attack success.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates provider-labeled hosted models and does not identify or apply a refusal-direction ablation or weight-edit recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: The hosted models score 91% and 89% on WMDP-Bio, scored on final answers rather than log-probs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Provider-labelled abliterated models can show high dual-use bio knowledge. Retention relative to the unabliterated models is not established.

fits_no_version.finding: Effective Dangerous Capability proxy (capability × compliance) of 83% and 88%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hosted abliterated models score highly on a combined bio capability-and-compliance proxy.

record.problems: The model identities, quantisation, and system prompts could not be independently verified because the endpoints are closed. Dangerous-prompt compliance was self-judged by the answering model. The Effective Dangerous Capability score is a proxy combining different question sets, and the author notes that the setup differs from FAR.AI's. There is no unabliterated baseline or direct test of the ablation procedure.
record.rows_left_out: No study result measuring an ablation intervention, added direction, attack suppression, training robustness, or other claim version was reported. The provider's Terminal-Bench comparison is attributed to the provider and was not included as a study result.

untested.parts: Whether the hosted models were actually made by a refusal-direction weight edit; refusal rates of the unabliterated originals; retention of capability against the base model. The Terminal-Bench figure is the provider's claim, not the study's result.
Not tested: no direction extraction, ablation or addition.

missing.what: Comparison against FAR.AI's own abliterated models. The author says compliance is comparable to or slightly lower than FAR.AI's best, and the higher aggregate comes mainly from capability. The numbers sit in graphs not present in the text.
missing.locator: Section 'Hosted models online match or exceed FAR.AI's tested models' (figures)

record.verdict_notes: This is a blog-style case study. Model identity, quantisation and system prompt are unverifiable, and the provider applies its own content filters (self-harm, CSAM). The compliance measure is StrongREJECT usefulness, self-judged, so it is only a proxy for refusal removal. The provider's Terminal-Bench claim (80.1% vs 81%) is correctly excluded from the rows.

versions.untested_parts: Does not find a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction, ablate or add it, or compare general abilities before and after intervention.
Does not independently verify that the hosted models use a weight edit or compare them with their unabliterated counterparts.
Does not test whether attacks suppress the direction or whether training against ablation improves robustness.
Does not test whether refusal is affine, conical, or carried by multiple directions.
Does not separate harmfulness judgment from refusal decisions.
Does not compare languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
Does not vary refusal-training methods or timing.
Does not test reasoning models against the V1 intervention.

relation.reason: The study's own compliance numbers bear on whether released abliterated models stop refusing. The test is weak: no unablated baseline, and the abliteration is not verified.

tranche.reason: A new setting: commercially hosted, provider-labelled abliterated models. It gives a direct result on V2: 92% and 99% useful compliance on explicitly dangerous bio requests. It does not use the method as a tool for its own method's performance, so it is not T4.

source_check.notes: The pack gives this verdict no [lN] id; label_id 'l1' was assigned by position. Read 92%/99% as compliance by provider-labelled hosted endpoints, not a measured effect of abliteration. The text never states a pre-abliteration refusal rate. The Terminal-Bench 80.1% vs 81% figure is the company's own claim, quoted rather than measured. The FAR.AI comparison is figure-only and called 'illustrative'.

statements.problem: None for this study. The statement gives no numbers for it. The 'unverified' reading fits: the provider applies the abliterated label, the author uses provider-declared names and cannot verify endpoint identity, quantisation or system prompt, and the author's 'abliterated skilfully' rests on the company's own benchmark claim.
